name: eBL Fragmentarium: the fragment database of the Electronic Babylonian Library (eBL) project at LMU Munich, led by Enrique Jiménez
date: Project began April 2018 with a Sofja Kovalevskaja Award from the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation. A public launch was first planned for autumn 2021; the Fragmentarium and the first digital eBL edition of Gilgamesh went public in February 2023. Main press coverage of the Gilgamesh results: LMU/phys.org (February 2023), Jiménez in The Conversation (25 May 2023), Erik Ofgang in the New York Times (12 August 2024). Follow-on work: Hymn to Babylon press release (28 July 2025) and an arXiv paper on automated sign detection across the eBL (21 June 2026). Sources: https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://phys.org/news/2023-02-ai-texts-thousands-years-readable.html ; https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091 ; https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/12/books/booksupdate/ai-ancient-tablets-gilgamesh.html ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22608
creator: Enrique Jiménez (Professor of Ancient Near Eastern Literatures, Institute of Assyriology, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität Munich) and the eBL team: developer J. Laasonen; contributors including L. Sáenz, E. Gogokhia, H. Stadhouders, A. C. Heinrich, Zs. Földi, T. Mitto and A. Hätinen; conservator C. Gütschow; translators Benjamin R. Foster (English) and Anmar A. Fadhil of the University of Baghdad (Arabic). Partners: the British Museum (liaison Jon Taylor), the Iraq Museum (liaison Anmar Fadhil), and the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities. Sources: https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/hymn-to-babylon-readable-again-thanks-to-ai-2ae70bee.html
form: Online dataset and search platform: a database of transliterated cuneiform fragments linked to museum photographs, stored as parsed JSON in MongoDB and lemmatised against the Concise Dictionary of Akkadian, with a fragment-matching search. It sits alongside the eBL Corpus, a digital edition of Babylonian literary texts, Gilgamesh among them. Sources: https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091
effect_on_arc: The finds are small, but several fall at points that matter for the characters. Reports of the NYT coverage list new material on Enkidu trying to talk Gilgamesh round over Humbaba, the pair's journey to Nippur after the Humbaba episode, a prayer by Gilgamesh's mother Ninsun to the sun god, and extra detail in Utnapishtim's flood story. The best-known change is one word. Utnapishtim now feeds the men building the boat in a 'prodigal' (or 'lavish') way, and Benjamin Foster reads it as guilt: 'he feels guilty because he knows that all the people helping him build the ark will be drowned in a few days.' That turns a stock detail into a moral one and makes the flood hero more human. Earlier eBL-era work by Jiménez (Iraq 76, 2014) placed Sm.209, part of one of Enkidu's speeches in the Humbaba episode. The late manuscript of c. 130 BC also changes the poem's own history: Gilgamesh was still being copied in the Hellenistic period, long after the Standard Babylonian version took shape. The Nippur and Ninsun details come from a secondary summary of the NYT piece [uncertain]. Sources: https://en.futuroprossimo.it/2024/08/epopea-di-gilgamesh-si-svela-lia-ricompone-il-puzzle-mesopotamico/ ; https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/12/books/booksupdate/ai-ancient-tablets-gilgamesh.html ; https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/49550/1/Jimenez_New_Fragments_of_Gilgames_and_other_Literary_Texts_from_Kuyunjik.pdf ; https://phys.org/news/2023-02-ai-texts-thousands-years-readable.html
critical_response: Coverage has been broadly admiring. The NYT (Erik Ofgang, 12 August 2024) said A.I. has brought an 'extreme acceleration' to the field. Artnet, Freethink, the Jerusalem Post, IFLScience and Ancient Origins ran versions of the same story. Jiménez's own estimate, given to phys.org, is that 'without the Fragmentarium, the reconstruction process would have taken 30, 40 years.' The Gilgamesh translator Sophus Helle, quoted in the coverage, described the text as 'so old and yet so alive', like 'painting a model that doesn't stand still'. The scholarly output is peer-reviewed and conventional: the 'From the Electronic Babylonian Literature Lab' notes in KASKAL, and articles such as 'Further Fragments of Gilgameš' (KASKAL 19, 2022). I found no substantive scholarly critique of the method itself [uncertain]. Sources: https://paleojudaica.blogspot.com/2024/08/ai-is-finding-more-gilgamesh-epic.html?m=1 ; https://phys.org/news/2023-02-ai-texts-thousands-years-readable.html ; https://en.futuroprossimo.it/2024/08/epopea-di-gilgamesh-si-svela-lia-ricompone-il-puzzle-mesopotamico/ ; https://www.academia.edu/121219115/Further_Fragments_of_Gilgame%C5%A1_Kaskal_19_2022_137_138
controversies: No dispute over accuracy or provenance has attached to the project. The friction is over the word 'A.I.' Popular reports describe an AI that deciphers tablets, and one outlet names the matching algorithm 'cuneiBLAST'. The matching the Gilgamesh finds rely on is a string-alignment algorithm run over transliterations that human Assyriologists typed from photographs. It is closer to bioinformatics sequence search than to a model reading clay. A separate machine-learning model for disambiguating signs (reported at 98 per cent accuracy) and later image-based sign detection are distinct pieces of work. Media numbers also drift between sources: '22,000 fragments', '21,000+ tablets', 'two-thirds' or '60%' of the poem reconstructed. The media conflation is my own reading of the sources, not a published critique [uncertain]. Sources: https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091 ; https://www.freethink.com/robots-ai/cuneiform-tablets ; https://phys.org/news/2023-02-ai-texts-thousands-years-readable.html
regional_reception: The project has an Iraqi partnership built in. The Iraq Museum is a formal partner, the eBL team has trained Iraq Museum conservators to treat tablets from the Sippar Library (excavated by Iraqi archaeologists in 1986), and Anmar A. Fadhil of the University of Baghdad is the project's Arabic translator and Jiménez's co-author on the Hymn to Babylon. LMU reports Iraqi colleagues telling Jiménez 'You make us proud to be Babylonians.' An Arabic translation of the eBL texts means the results can be read in the region, though I did not confirm how much of the Gilgamesh edition is in Arabic [uncertain]. Sources: https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://www.lmu.de/en/newsroom/news-overview/news/hymn-to-babylon-readable-again-thanks-to-ai-2ae70bee.html
method: Mostly human cuneiform scholarship made searchable. Team members transliterate fragments from museum photographs (above all the British Museum's Kuyunjik and Babylon collections) into the database. A string-alignment algorithm adapted for cuneiform, like the sequence alignment used in genetics, then compares each fragment's text against everything else in the Fragmentarium and the Corpus. It allows for spelling variants, since one syllable can be written up to 25 ways. Suggested matches are checked by an Assyriologist and, where possible, confirmed as physical joins or as new manuscripts of a known text. A separate model trained on fewer than 20,000 lines, without sign lists, disambiguates cuneiform readings with about 98 per cent success. Since 2025/26 the group has also built image-based sign detection (OCR) across the eBL photographs. Sources: https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091 ; https://www.freethink.com/robots-ai/cuneiform-tablets ; https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22608
ai_pipeline_stage: Fragment matching: the machine proposes which pieces belong to which text. Imaging is done by museum photographers and first transliteration by humans. Translation is human (Foster in English, Fadhil in Arabic). Sign recognition from photographs is newer and experimental: a 2026 paper by Che, Garcés Arias, Niaz, Bender and Jiménez ran a detection transformer over 87,668 eBL fragments and produced about 2.9 million sign detections. Sources: https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091 ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22608
scale_metrics: About 13,500 fragments and 140,000 lines transliterated by February 2020, with 75% of unpublished Nineveh fragments covered. About 17,500 fragments and 215,000+ lines by February 2021. Nearly 22,000 fragments by the February 2023 launch, with over 300,000 lines reported by Freethink. Joins: about 5,000 made across 150 years of Assyriology before 2018, then 1,500+ more by the eBL team since 2018, plus several thousand further pieces placed. Gilgamesh: 20 new fragments adding to more than 100 lines (NYT, 2024), and roughly two-thirds of the text now reconstructed. Latest datable Gilgamesh manuscript: c. 130 BC. The Hymn to Babylon was rebuilt from 15 new fragments. About 200 scholars had access before the public launch. By 2026 the eBL image corpus used for sign detection held 87,668 fragments. Some 500,000 cuneiform tablets are thought to be in museum collections. Sources: https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://phys.org/news/2023-02-ai-texts-thousands-years-readable.html ; https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091 ; https://paleojudaica.blogspot.com/2024/08/ai-is-finding-more-gilgamesh-epic.html?m=1 ; https://www.freethink.com/robots-ai/cuneiform-tablets ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22608
what_was_found: Twenty unplaced fragments identified as Gilgamesh, adding text to more than 100 lines. They include a manuscript copied around 130 BC, the latest known. Reported new content covers Enkidu's attempts to persuade Gilgamesh over Humbaba, the journey to Nippur after the Humbaba episode, Ninsun's prayer to Shamash, and more of Utnapishtim's flood account in Tablet XI, including the word for his 'prodigal' feeding of the boat-builders. Jiménez's earlier Kuyunjik work (2014) identified three new Gilgamesh fragments, among them Sm.209 with part of an Enkidu speech from the Humbaba episode (proposed as manuscript H3). All of it feeds the eBL Corpus edition of Gilgamesh, the first to gather every known manuscript. The exact tablet and museum number of the 130 BC manuscript were not confirmed [uncertain]. Sources: https://en.futuroprossimo.it/2024/08/epopea-di-gilgamesh-si-svela-lia-ricompone-il-puzzle-mesopotamico/ ; https://phys.org/news/2023-02-ai-texts-thousands-years-readable.html ; https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/49550/1/Jimenez_New_Fragments_of_Gilgames_and_other_Literary_Texts_from_Kuyunjik.pdf
provenance_and_ethics: The source material is legitimate museum holdings. Most comes from the British Museum's Kuyunjik (Nineveh, Ashurbanipal's library) and Babylon collections, excavated in the 19th century and still in London; the rest comes from the Iraq Museum's Sippar Library tablets, excavated in Iraq in 1986 and held in Baghdad. The project does not buy or handle looted material. It works from photographs of registered collections, and much of its Iraq work is conservation and training for Iraq Museum staff. The objects stay with their museums while the digital transliterations live in the eBL at LMU Munich; photographs belong to the lending museums. So the Nineveh fragments are joined digitally in Munich while the clay stays in London, a split that mirrors the colonial-era removal of the tablets. I did not confirm the exact licence terms for eBL data or images [uncertain]. Sources: https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/ ; https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/49550/1/Jimenez_New_Fragments_of_Gilgames_and_other_Literary_Texts_from_Kuyunjik.pdf
ai_craft_tension: The Fragmentarium is a good case of a machine doing the drudgery and a person doing the reading. The algorithm is tireless at one narrow job: take a string of damaged signs and find where else in 22,000 fragments that sequence, or a spelling variant of it, turns up. That is the job George Smith did by eye in the 1870s, and it is why 1,500 joins arrived in about five years after 5,000 in a century and a half. Everything on either side is still human. Someone had to transliterate each fragment from a photograph before the search could run. Someone has to check the suggested match against the clay, decide which tablet and column it belongs to, and translate it. The part that makes a find matter, seeing that 'prodigal' feeding of doomed workers means Utnapishtim feels guilty, is Foster's reading, not the algorithm's. Popular coverage says 'A.I. deciphers Gilgamesh'. The more honest line is that the machine finds the pieces faster, and the meaning still comes from someone who knows the poem.
essay_hooks: (1) 5,000 joins in 150 years of Assyriology, then 1,500+ in about five years with the Fragmentarium (Jiménez, The Conversation, 2023). (2) 'Without the Fragmentarium, the reconstruction process would have taken 30, 40 years' (Jiménez, phys.org, February 2023). (3) One syllable can be written up to 25 ways in cuneiform, which is why plain text search fails. (4) The latest Gilgamesh copy dates to about 130 BC: 'people were still copying Gilgamesh at this late period' (Jiménez). (5) A single new word, 'prodigal', gives the flood hero a conscience: 'he feels guilty because he knows that all the people helping him build the ark will be drowned in a few days' (Benjamin Foster, via NYT coverage, 2024). (6) The method borrows from genetics: sequence alignment like that used on DNA, applied to clay. (7) Iraqi colleagues to Jiménez: 'You make us proud to be Babylonians' (LMU, July 2025). (8) Contrast with Smith: the same Kuyunjik drawers he sorted by hand are now being searched by an algorithm.
